title: Cyanide and iodoethane
subtitle: Cyanide makes a new C–C bond

reactants.caption: cyanide + iodoethane
reactants.learnerPrompt: Draw the arrows for the single, concerted substitution step.
hintTiers: Cyanide is the nucleophile. Which carbon of iodoethane is electron-poor, and what is the leaving group?
The carbon of cyanide attacks the CH₂ carbon from the side opposite iodine, and the C–I bond breaks at the same time. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: the lone pair on cyanide's carbon forms a new bond to the CH₂ carbon. Arrow 2: the C–I bond breaks, and its pair goes onto iodine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Nitrogen can attack too, giving a little of the isonitrile, EtN≡C. But the carbon end of cyanide is the better nucleophile, so the nitrile is the main product.
The CH₃ carbon carries no leaving group. Attack the carbon bonded to iodine.
Iodine is the leaving group. The nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbon bonded to it, not the iodine itself.
The C–I pair leaves with iodine, which can hold a negative charge. It does not stay on carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Octet check: carbon would now have 10 electrons. What has to leave as the nucleophile arrives?
Iodide does leave, but a primary carbocation is far too unstable to form on its own. SN2 is concerted: the nucleophile pushes in at the same time.

steps.explanationAfterStep: One concerted step: the new C–C bond forms as the C–I bond breaks. Iodide is an excellent leaving group, and a polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO leaves cyanide poorly solvated and reactive.

mechanismSummary: SN2 with a carbon nucleophile: the chain grows by one carbon. Cyanide attacks through carbon, from the side opposite the C–I bond, in a single step; the rate depends on both cyanide and iodoethane.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 15
